summary.title: Tracking multiple objects with OpenCV
summary.one_liner: You learn to track several objects in video at once in Python by adding one OpenCV single-object tracker per object to a cv2.MultiTracker, and why this doesn't speed up the pipeline.
keywords: track multiple objects in video python
how to track many objects with opencv
takeaways: Create one OpenCV tracker instance per object and add each to a cv2.MultiTracker with its initial bounding box.
Select objects interactively with cv2.selectROI by pressing 's' in the loop; a detector would replace this in real systems.
KCF is fast and accurate, CSRT is more accurate but slower, and MOSSE is extremely fast but less accurate, per the author.
Each added tracker costs computation, so FPS drops roughly with the number of tracked objects; the MultiTracker class is a convenience, not a speedup.
The author notes only one CPU core is used and says parallel processing across cores is covered in a later post.
summary.summary: The tutorial builds a Python script that tracks multiple objects in a video or webcam feed using OpenCV 3.2+ and imutils. The user presses 's' to draw a bounding box around each object with cv2.selectROI, and each box gets its own single-object tracker added to a cv2.MultiTracker, which updates all boxes per frame. The author compares the available tracker types, then shows results on soccer, NASCAR and traffic clips. It closes by explaining that per-object trackers slow the pipeline and that the MultiTracker does not add speed, with multiprocessing deferred to a future post.
